cim: Már két német bíróság szerint is felelős a Google az AI-válaszaiért
lead: A müncheni és az aacheni bíróság szerint is a Google saját tartalmának számítanak az AI Overviews által generált válaszok.
osszefoglalo:
Újabb németországi ítélet mondta ki, hogy a Google közvetlenül felelős a keresőjében megjelenő mesterséges intelligencia által generált válaszokért. Az aacheni tartományi bíróság egy orvos ügyében hozott sürgősségi végzést, akiről a Google AI-ja tévesen azt állította, hogy szexuális zaklatás miatt bocsátották el. Az AI egy másik személy bűncselekményét kötötte a doktor nevéhez, és részletes, kitalált jogi eljárásokat jelenített meg róla.

A bíróság az előző, müncheni ítéletre támaszkodva megállapította, hogy az [AI Overviews](https://support.google.com/websearch/answer/14901683) nem csupán harmadik felek információit teszi kereshetővé, hanem önálló, új tartalomnak számít. Mivel a Google saját kijelentéseiként kezelik ezeket az összefoglalókat, a cégnek vállalnia kell a felelősséget a hamis állításokért. Amennyiben a Google megszegi a tilalmat, jogsértésenként akár 250 000 eurós bírsággal is sújtható.

A döntés hosszú távon alapjaiban kérdőjelezheti meg az AI-alapú keresők működési modelljét Németországban. Ha az AI-válaszok a cég saját tartalmának minősülnek, a tartalomgyártók és kiadók is díjazást követelhetnek az anyagaik felhasználásáért. A Google korábban a müncheni ügyben egyezséget kötött, hogy elkerülje a felsőbb bírósági ítéletet, de a jogi érvelés az újabb döntéssel tovább erősödött.
miert_szamit: A döntés előrevetíti, hogy az AI-eszközöket fejlesztő cégek **jogi felelősséggel tartoznak a halucinált vagy téves információkért**, ami szigorúbb ellenőrzési folyamatokhoz és a tartalomtulajdonosok jogainak erősödéséhez vezethet.

cim_eredeti: Two German courts now hold Google liable for what its AI overviews say
szoveg_eredeti:
Google tried to overturn a landmark Munich ruling on liability for AI search summaries by appealing, then quietly settled. Now a second court has applied the same reasoning. Google's AI answers count as the company's own content, and Google is responsible for them.

In late May, the Munich Regional Court I ruled in a widely watched case that Google is directly liable for the content of its AI-generated search summaries. Google's AI had falsely linked two Munich-based publishers to fraud schemes. The judges classified AI Overviews not as mere search results but as Google's own statements, meaning the company itself has to answer for them.

Instead of hiding behind the role of a neutral middleman passing along third-party information, Google would have to own the unlawful statements its AI produces. For a search feature that constantly generates new answers, that's a legal risk that's hard to quantify. If this view holds up, it could call into question the entire business model of AI search in Germany and shape the debate in other countries too.Ad

The distinction between a search reference and original content could also have consequences beyond false factual claims. If AI answers count as Google's own content, the publishers whose texts Google uses to generate those answers might eventually assert their own claims. That wasn't part of the Munich case, but it's a logical next step.Ad

As THE DECODER has learned, the appeal Google publicly announced was never carried through to a decision. The case ended in a settlement instead, meaning no higher court ever weighed in on the Munich reasoning. Why the settlement was reached and whether money changed hands is unknown. Neither Google nor the affected publisher would comment. The court also declined to weigh in on the broader significance of its own ruling beyond this specific case.

The Munich judges' legal reasoning isn't dead, though. In a decision dated September 24, 2026, the Aachen Regional Court barred Google from spreading certain false statements and explicitly relied on the Munich ruling's reasoning. Google can challenge the injunction. The decision isn't final yet.Ad

In this new case, a physician in Aachen fought back against serious false claims in Google's "AI Mode" search feature. The doctor had worked as chief physician and professor of neuroradiology from 2010 until late June 2026. On August 28, a colleague alerted him that Google's AI was explaining his departure by citing an alleged sexual assault against his secretary. When users ran additional searches using terms like "suspension," "termination," and "court proceedings," AI Mode returned detailed, multi-paragraph fabrications. It even invented a complete legal aftermath.

None of the allegations or proceedings had anything to do with the doctor. The AI had taken events involving a different former university professor and pinned them on him, something the Aachen court could confirm from its own records since the criminal case had actually been brought against someone else. Cases of AI misattribution like this have been documented before.Ad

Even though the doctor described the mix-up in detail in late August and asked Google by email to remove the content, the company said in mid-September that it would take no action. A formal legal demand sent the same day also went nowhere. Google confirmed receiving it, but according to the court, the false AI-generated texts were still live.Ad

The Aachen Regional Court then banned further spread of the three disputed text variants. Because the false claims could seriously damage the doctor's professional reputation, the court acted on an emergency basis without hearing Google first. If Google violates the order, it faces fines of up to 250,000 euros per violation.
